extracted.intended_audience: government acquisition analysts, program managers, and decisionmakers performing OMB A-76 cost comparisons for IT systems (Navy/DoD context)
extracted.subtask_description: Performing an OMB Circular A-76 style cost comparison to decide whether to continue in-house operation of the HRMIN system or to convert to a commercial/timesharing service; includes site-alternative evaluation, cost-element accounting, benchmarking, and sensitivity/assumption statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uses of Economic Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A cost comparison is a form of economic analysis. Such analyses are used in two ways: to assess the economic consequences of a decision already made, or as part of the decisionmaking process to compare the economic consequences of two or more alternatives as input to decision making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether the analysis is retrospective (assessing a decision already made) or prospective (comparing alternatives to inform a choice); choose model and scope accordingly (see Figure 5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with OMB Circular No. A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: The model used for this comparison is as specified in Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular No. A-76, Revised of 5 April 1979 (Acquiring of Commercial or Industrial Products and Service Needed by the Government; Policy Revision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the Circular's policies and procedures to determine whether work should be done in-house or contracted out; consult the Circular/appendices for detailed methodology rather than reproducing it in full.

rubrics_metrics.name: A-76 Policy Precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Three precepts: (1) the Government's business is not to be in business, (2) certain functions are inherently governmental and must be performed by federal employees, (3) the American people are entitled to economy in Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a function is not inherently governmental and a public sector org can do it, a cost comparison must identify the least costly method to the taxpayer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Assumptions of the Cost Comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost comparison will be structured to account for all pertinent costs that will be affected by an alternative selection. Costs related to management and operation at the Program Manager's location and at user sites will not be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state base year (here FY 1982), assumptions about inflation (assumed equal across alternatives), unchanged system requirements, and which costs are excluded; document data sources and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: System Performance and Reliability (site-evaluation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: System performance was defined as how well the system supports and performs the function of the application running on it. System reliability was defined as the ability of a system to provide dependable support on a continuous basis (90% up-time and a back-up system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess uptime, backup capability, and functional support for application workloads when comparing location/operation alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: System and Data Security (site-evaluation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Security was defined as providing an acceptable level of protection against unauthorized access to the system and to HRM Survey data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the alternative's ability to protect system and data from unauthorized access; account for security controls and operational constraints (not just raw cost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Management Control (site-evaluation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The key management control factor for any alternative is the ease with which the sponsor can monitor the performance of the system and if necessary re-direct the management or content of the application so that the plans or objectives for the system are effectively used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how readily the sponsor can oversee, intervene, or redirect operations under each alternative; include interface/coordination costs if material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance and Operational Support (site-evaluation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of the managing organization at the location to provide adequate personnel resources for the maintenance and operation of the system hardware and software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess availability of qualified staff, transition/training needs, expected staffing levels, and ongoing support capability at each alternative location or vendor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost (site-evaluation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost was the final criterion used to evaluate the alternative locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although listed last, cost is decisive in the comparative analysis; note rating legend: criteria are in descending order of importance to interviewed personnel, and for cost a higher rating means lower costs (i.e., 'high' = cost-beneficial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking as Vendor Evaluation Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmarking is the method of evaluating potential vendors during competitive procurement: a benchmark is a mix of requirements representative of the user's projected workload; mandatory and desired specifications and test programs are presented in the RFP; potential clients run the benchmark job and are graded using a scheme devised by the proposer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use representative programs and workload, include mandatory/desired specs in RFP, define grading scheme up front; recognize benchmarking limitations (e.g., negotiation/discounts may materially affect final prices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendor Cost Factors for Timesharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Vendors base charges on connect time, CPU time (processing), storage capacity, channel time, and additional charges (file access, languages, application programs, terminal and communication equipment rentals, royalties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing timesharing bids, itemize and reconcile these charge bases; be alert to usage-sensitive elements (connect/CPU/time-varying charges) and vendor-specific add-ons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical Benefits of Contracting/Timesharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits include fewer programming errors, no training required, known costs, no equipment maintenance, minimum personnel problems, increased experience and capability for future efforts, and greater capability for handling varying workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualitatively weigh these non-monetary benefits against in-house advantages; where possible, translate into monetized or risk-adjusted terms or note as decision factors outside base-year cost comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical Disadvantages of Timesharing / Contracting
rubrics_metrics.description: Disadvantages include being needlessly expensive for some users, increased communications charges for data-heavy workloads, added overhead/marketing/administration/profit in vendor pricing, potential usage delays due to lines or vendor systems, and accentuated data security problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the profile of system use (e.g., need for quick responses, high transaction volume, sensitive data) makes timesharing unsuitable or riskier despite apparent cost figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Low Bidder and Bid Validity
rubrics_metrics.description: The low bidder is not considered if the bid appears to be a 'buy-in' quote (not representative of true cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Screen bids for realism; discard or scrutinize anomalously low quotes that may not include full service commitments or recurring costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Labor (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct labor: actual or estimated personnel positions and salaries required for an operational system (e.g., System Manager GS-12 full time, Analyst/Programmer GS-11 full time, Computer Operator GS-7 full time, Research Psychologist GS-15 full time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic staffing assumptions for operational posture (not prorated development time); document grades, FTEs, and calculations transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fringe Benefits on Labor (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringe benefit costs: e.g., FY1982 fringe benefits were $31,357.55; analysis assumes permanent GS employees with retirement but no FICA, no holiday premium pay, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate fringe benefit rates tied to the assumed labor classification; state assumptions about employee status that affect benefit rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead (cost element) and its subcomponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations overhead consists of indirect labor, indirect materials and supplies, depreciation, rent, maintenance and repair, support costs, utilities, and insurance. The example totals operations overhead at $124,580.70 (FY82).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break out each subcomponent; identify which items are aggregated into G&A vs charged directly; specify data sources and any estimates (e.g., maintenance contract increases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depreciation Method and Treatment of Capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Straight line depreciation is used over estimated useful life (author assumes five years). For this cost comparison, capital costs are 'sunk' and not considered if the capital will be owned by the government by the time of analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State depreciation method and lives; treat only relevant capital costs (exclude sunk costs) unless comparing acquisition alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Direct Costs (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other direct costs include annual software royalties (SPSS), travel, training, and telecommunications (fixed + variable), totaling example value $55,450.00 for FY1982.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include recurring software fees, travel/training, and telecom usage; model telecom as usage-sensitive and run sensitivity scenarios for utilization changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: General and Administrative Expenses (G&A) (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: G&A expense pool charges a portion of the pool to each cost center (example: Code 205 $17,268; Code 16 $14,219; total $31,487 for FY1982).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate G&A consistently and transparently; document cost-center basis and any assumptions about self-sufficiency or allocation rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of Capital (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opportunity cost of capital is computed using net book value of capital assets and an opportunity/discount rate (example: net book value $227,848 and 10% rate gives $22,785).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include an explicit opportunity cost calculation where relevant; state discount/opportunity rate and book values used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflation and One-Time Costs (treatment rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflation and One-Time and Other Costs are not germane to this base-year comparison because the analysis examines the base year only of a system already running.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State whether inflation/out-year costs or one-time transition costs are included or excluded; if excluded, explain rationale and consider appendix sensitivity or present-value methods if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: User Profile Determination and Usage Metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive a user profile from system job accounting and network records (e.g., HARRIS job accounting, Tymnet records). Example: sum allocated connect time and CPU time to compute annual connect hours and connect:CPU ratio (example: 1,598h20m allocated; 223h47m CPU; connect:CPU = 7.14:1; postulated real yearly connect time = 4,740.5 hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the most current and representative usage data; justify any postulated adjustments (e.g., future user activation not considered) and document calculation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment of Benchmarked Vendor Costs Using Real Usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust vendor benchmark connect/processing charges by comparing vendor 'worst-case' benchmark hours to the postulated in-house real hours. Example: Tymshare benchmark 13,695 hours divided by postulated 4,740 hours yields an adjustment factor 2.9 (vendor benchmark 2.9 times too high).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply adjustment factors transparently and justify assumptions (e.g., charge rates used to derive vendor hours); apply same factor only when vendor rate assumptions are comparable; quantify sensitivity to this adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and Sensitivity of Benchmarking and Negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: Large differences in contract prices can be driven by negotiations and bidders' internal pricing policies; benchmarking has serious limitations because competitive bidding and negotiation skills greatly affect final costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge benchmarking limitations explicitly; perform sensitivity analyses, consider alternative vendor pricing scenarios, and document negotiation/discount assumptions.
